blocks.text: A blood test shows two numbers that tell the whole story of an endocrine gland: the hormone the gland makes, and the pituitary hormone that is trying to control it. If thyroxine is low and TSH is high, the thyroid is failing and the pituitary is shouting; if both are low, the fault lies higher up. Negative feedback loops turn two blood results into a diagnosis.

blocks.markdown: **The idea of an axis.** An endocrine axis is a three-tier chain: a hypothalamic hormone stimulates a pituitary hormone, which stimulates a peripheral gland, and the peripheral hormone feeds back to inhibit the two upstream tiers. Two such axes are examined here, the **hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis** and the **hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid (HPT) axis**. Because the loop is closed, changing one component in a predictable direction changes the others in predictable directions.

blocks.title: Negative feedback in an axis
blocks.text: Negative feedback means that the end product of a chain inhibits the steps that produce it. In the HPA axis, cortisol inhibits CRH and ACTH. In the HPT axis, T3 and T4 inhibit TRH and TSH. A failing peripheral gland therefore causes a rise in the pituitary hormone (loss of feedback), whereas a failing pituitary causes a fall in both.

blocks.markdown:
**The HPA axis.** Neurons in the **paraventricular nucleus** secrete **corticotrophin-releasing hormone (CRH)** into the portal system. CRH stimulates **corticotrophs** of the anterior pituitary to release **ACTH** (adrenocorticotropic hormone, cleaved from pro-opiomelanocortin). ACTH acts on the **adrenal cortex**, mainly the **zona fasciculata**, to stimulate **cortisol** synthesis from cholesterol and also maintains the size of the cortex (it is trophic). Cortisol inhibits CRH and ACTH release at both the hypothalamus and pituitary. Secretion follows a **circadian rhythm** (peak around the time of waking, lowest around midnight) and rises with stress, when the CRH drive overrides feedback. About 90% of circulating cortisol is bound to **corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG)**; only the free fraction is active.

Clinically, adrenal failure from gland destruction (primary) gives **low cortisol with high ACTH**; failure of the pituitary (secondary) gives **low cortisol with low ACTH**.

blocks.caption: f_bound is the fraction bound to carrier proteins such as CBG or thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG); only the free fraction acts on target cells and feeds back.

blocks.title: Free cortisol when binding protein changes
blocks.prompt: A woman's total serum cortisol is 600 nmol/L and 90% is bound to CBG. Calculate her free cortisol. If a rise in CBG (as in pregnancy or oestrogen therapy) increases the total to 900 nmol/L with 94% bound, what is the new free cortisol, and what does this show?

steps.text: The total cortisol is 50% higher but the free cortisol has not risen, so the axis is not hyperactive: total hormone concentration can be misleading when carrier protein changes.

blocks.answer: Free cortisol is 60 nmol/L at baseline and 54 nmol/L after CBG rises, so the apparent increase in total cortisol reflects more binding protein, not more active hormone.

blocks.markdown:
**Thyroid hormone synthesis.** The thyroid is made of **follicles**: a ring of follicular cells around a lumen of **colloid** rich in the protein **thyroglobulin**. The steps are:

1. **Iodide uptake** against a gradient by the Na+/I- symporter (NIS) on the basolateral membrane, then transfer to the colloid.
2. **Oxidation and organification:** thyroid peroxidase (TPO) oxidises iodide and iodinates tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin to give monoiodotyrosine (MIT) and diiodotyrosine (DIT).
3. **Coupling:** TPO joins DIT + DIT to make **T4 (thyroxine)** and MIT + DIT to make **T3**; the hormones remain bound in thyroglobulin as stored colloid.
4. **Release:** TSH stimulates endocytosis of colloid, proteolysis of thyroglobulin and secretion of mainly **T4** (about 90%), with some T3.

Peripheral tissues convert T4 to the more active **T3** by **deiodinases**. In plasma more than 99% of thyroid hormone is bound to **thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG)** and other proteins; the small free fraction is active and is what the pituitary senses. Thyroid peroxidase is the target of antithyroid drugs (a pharmacology teaching example), and iodine deficiency causes goitre through chronic TSH stimulation.

Excess thyroid hormone inhibits pituitary; stimulating antibodies mimic TSH

blocks.markdown: **Actions of thyroid hormones.** T3 binds nuclear receptors and alters gene expression. The main effects are to **raise basal metabolic rate** and heat production (including increased Na+/K+ ATPase), to increase **heart rate and contractility** (more beta-adrenergic receptors), to increase gut motility, and to promote **growth and brain development** in children. Hypothyroid patients therefore tend to be cold, slow, constipated and bradycardic, with weight gain and a goitre or a small gland, depending on the cause; hyperthyroid patients are heat-intolerant, have weight loss despite appetite, tremor, tachycardia and diarrhoea.

blocks.title: Predicting the pattern in a failing pituitary
blocks.prompt: A tumour destroys the thyrotrophs of the anterior pituitary but the thyroid is normal. Predict TSH, free T4, and the effect on the size of the thyroid, and explain why this differs from primary hypothyroidism.

steps.text: Thyrotroph destruction removes TSH, so TSH is low.
Without TSH, the thyroid receives no stimulation and secretes less hormone, so free T4 is low.
TSH also maintains thyroid follicular cell size, so the gland will shrink (atrophy) rather than enlarge, and there is no goitre.
In primary hypothyroidism the pituitary is intact, so low T4 removes feedback and TSH is high; in central hypothyroidism both are low.

blocks.answer: TSH low, free T4 low, thyroid atrophic; the low TSH distinguishes central from primary hypothyroidism.

items: Adrenal cortex releases cortisol; thyroid releases T4 and T3.
Free hormone acts on target tissues and feeds back to inhibit the hypothalamus and pituitary.
Failure at the gland raises the pituitary hormone; failure at the pituitary lowers both.

blocks.title: Two numbers decide the level of the lesion
blocks.text: Always interpret the pituitary hormone alongside the peripheral hormone. Low T4 with high TSH is primary thyroid failure; low T4 with low or normal TSH is central; high T4 with suppressed TSH is primary hyperthyroidism. The same logic applies to cortisol and ACTH.

blocks.title: Binding proteins change the total, not the free level
blocks.text: Pregnancy and oestrogen therapy raise TBG and CBG, so total T4 and total cortisol rise while free hormone and TSH remain normal. Do not diagnose hyperthyroidism or Cushing syndrome from total concentrations alone.

points: The HPA axis runs CRH to ACTH to cortisol, with cortisol feeding back on hypothalamus and pituitary; secretion has a circadian rhythm, and ACTH also maintains the adrenal cortex.
Thyroid hormone synthesis requires iodide uptake (NIS), TPO-mediated iodination and coupling on thyroglobulin, and TSH-driven release of T4 (mostly) and T3.
T4 is converted to the active T3 in tissues, and only the free fraction is active; T3 raises metabolic rate, heart rate and supports growth.
Primary hypothyroidism gives low free T4 and high TSH; primary hyperthyroidism gives high free T4 and suppressed TSH; central disease gives low T4 with low or inappropriately normal TSH.

questions.stem: Which pituitary hormone stimulates cortisol secretion from the adrenal cortex?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ACTH from corticotrophs acts on the adrenal cortex.
distractorRationale.c: CRH is the hypothalamic hormone that stimulates ACTH release, not the pituitary hormone.

questions.explanation: CRH from the hypothalamus stimulates corticotrophs to release ACTH, which acts on the adrenal cortex to stimulate cortisol synthesis. Cortisol then feeds back negatively on the hypothalamus and pituitary.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man has autoimmune destruction of both adrenal cortices. Which pattern is expected?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: loss of negative feedback drives ACTH up.
distractorRationale.b: This is the pattern of pituitary (secondary) failure.
distractorRationale.c: This would suggest an autonomous cortisol-secreting adrenal tumour.
distractorRationale.d: This suggests an ACTH-secreting source driving the adrenals.

questions.explanation: When the adrenal glands fail, cortisol falls, so the negative feedback on CRH and ACTH is lost and ACTH rises. The high ACTH distinguishes primary from secondary adrenal insufficiency.

questions.stem: Which enzyme is required to iodinate tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin and to couple them to make thyroid hormones?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: TPO oxidises iodide, iodinates tyrosines and couples MIT and DIT.
distractorRationale.c: 5'-deiodinase converts T4 to T3 in peripheral tissues.
distractorRationale.d: Carbonic anhydrase catalyses CO2 and water interconversion.

questions.explanation: Thyroid peroxidase catalyses oxidation of iodide, iodination of tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin and coupling of iodotyrosines to give T4 and T3. It is the site of action of antithyroid drugs and a common autoantigen.

questions.stem: Which statement about the conversion of thyroid hormones is correct?

options.text: Most thyroid output is T4, which is converted in peripheral tissues to the more active T3
Most thyroid output is T3, which is converted to T4 in the liver
T4 is more potent than T3 at the nuclear receptor
Thyroid hormones circulate mainly in the free form

questions.correctOptionText: Most thyroid output is T4, which is converted in peripheral tissues to the more active T3

distractorRationale.a: Correct: T4 acts partly as a prohormone.
distractorRationale.b: The direction of conversion is the reverse: T4 to T3.
distractorRationale.c: T3 is the more active form at the receptor.
distractorRationale.d: More than 99% is bound to TBG and other proteins.

questions.explanation: The thyroid secretes mostly T4 (about 90%), and deiodinases in tissues remove an iodine atom to form T3, the more active hormone. More than 99% of both circulates protein-bound.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman has tiredness, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance and a pulse of 52/min. Which results are most expected?

options.text: Low free T4 and high TSH
High free T4 and low TSH
Low free T4 and low TSH
Normal free T4 and high ACTH

questions.correctOptionText: Low free T4 and high TSH

distractorRationale.a: Correct: primary hypothyroidism with loss of negative feedback gives high TSH.
distractorRationale.b: This is the pattern of primary hyperthyroidism.
distractorRationale.c: This is the pattern of central hypothyroidism, which is less common.
distractorRationale.d: ACTH is not the marker of thyroid function.

questions.explanation: The symptoms indicate a low metabolic rate. In primary hypothyroidism the gland cannot produce enough T4, negative feedback on the pituitary is reduced, and TSH rises; this is the usual pattern and TSH is the key first-line test.

questions.stem: In primary hyperthyroidism, such as Graves disease, serum TSH is characteristically suppressed.
questions.explanation: Excess free T4 and T3 inhibit the pituitary and hypothalamus by negative feedback, so TSH is low. In Graves disease, antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor drive thyroid hormone production independently of TSH.

questions.stem: A patient's total serum cortisol is 450 nmol/L, of which 90% is bound to corticosteroid-binding globulin. What is the free cortisol concentration in nmol/L?
questions.explanation: If 90% is bound, 10% is free, so free cortisol is 0.10 x 450 = 45 nmol/L. Only this free fraction is biologically active and exerts feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary.

questions.stem: A patient's total T4 is 90 nmol/L, of which 99.98% is bound to plasma proteins. Calculate the free T4 concentration in pmol/L (1 nmol = 1000 pmol).
questions.explanation: The free fraction is 100% - 99.98% = 0.02% = 0.0002. Free T4 = 0.0002 x 90 nmol/L = 0.018 nmol/L = 18 pmol/L. Only this tiny fraction is active and is the fraction the pituitary senses, which is why free T4 is preferred to total T4.

questions.stem: Describe the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, naming the hormones and their sites of origin, and explain how negative feedback, circadian rhythm and stress modify it.
markingGuide: CRH is secreted by hypothalamic paraventricular neurons into the portal system
CRH stimulates pituitary corticotrophs to release ACTH (from POMC)
ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex (zona fasciculata) to make cortisol and maintains adrenal cortex size
Cortisol feeds back negatively on both the hypothalamus (CRH) and pituitary (ACTH)
Circadian rhythm: cortisol peaks in the early morning around waking and is lowest around midnight
Stress increases CRH drive and overrides feedback, raising cortisol
Cortisol is mostly bound to CBG; only free cortisol is active
questions.explanation: The HPA axis is a classic negative feedback loop with an overlaid rhythm and stress input. Understanding the loop lets you predict ACTH in primary versus secondary adrenal disease.

questions.stem: Outline the synthesis, release and peripheral activation of thyroid hormones, then predict the TSH and free T4 results in primary hypothyroidism, primary hyperthyroidism and central hypothyroidism, explaining each.
markingGuide: Iodide is taken up by the Na+/I- symporter and moved to colloid
Thyroid peroxidase oxidises iodide and iodinates tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin to give MIT and DIT, then couples them to T4 and T3
TSH stimulates endocytosis of colloid, proteolysis of thyroglobulin and release of mainly T4
Peripheral deiodinases convert T4 to the more active T3; most hormone is protein-bound with the free fraction active
Primary hypothyroidism: low free T4 and high TSH because negative feedback is lost
Primary hyperthyroidism: high free T4 with suppressed TSH because excess hormone inhibits the pituitary
Central hypothyroidism: low free T4 with low or inappropriately normal TSH because the pituitary or hypothalamus is failing
questions.explanation: The direction of the TSH change relative to free T4 shows where the lesion lies. This follows directly from the feedback loop and the synthetic pathway.
